# Static JavaScript Asset Assessment Methodology for External Web Application Assessment - Hypothesis Generation Phase Only This methodology is advisory and reusable. It does not assert findings about any target. All checks described are future validation steps. Unknown target conditions are treated as future checks, not observed results. ## Scope and Asset Definition Asset class: vendor script files served via GET with no inputs, MIME type application/javascript, and no dynamic processing. Prerequisites for inclusion: 1. Asset is discoverable via HTTP GET request with a stable URL. 2. Response header Content-Type is application/javascript or text/javascript. 3. Response body is static; no query parameters, path parameters, or request headers alter the served bytes. 4. Asset is referenced from an in-scope origin or is a third-party vendor script loaded by in-scope pages. 5. Assessment scope permits external asset review and passive analysis. Assumptions: - The asset is static at assessment time. Caching, versioning, or build pipelines may change content later. - No server-side processing occurs for the request. Dynamic generation would move the asset out of scope. - The assessor has read access to the asset bytes via GET. - Execution context, DOM, and page interactions are not in scope for this static-only phase. Unknowns to be resolved as future checks: - Whether the asset is actually static for all request variants. - Whether integrity controls such as Subresource Integrity are applied at the referencing page. - Whether the asset is executed in a privileged context or with sensitive data. - Whether the vendor script is updated independently of the assessed application. ## Prerequisite Verification for Static Serving Before any hypothesis is applied, confirm the static-serving prerequisite with a documented stability check. Future verification procedure: 1. Record baseline request: GET identical URL with no query string, Accept: */*, User-Agent generic, no Cookie, no Authorization. Record response code, Content-Type, Content-Length, ETag/Last-Modified, and a hash of body. 2. Repeat GET with representative variant headers: Accept: application/javascript, Accept-Encoding: gzip, br; User-Agent variants; Cache-Control: no-cache, max-age=0; Pragma: no-cache. 3. Repeat GET with common request header variations that sometimes trigger dynamic behavior, e.g., Accept-Language, Sec-Fetch-* headers. 4. Decision rule for static classification: All variant requests return 200 with identical Content-Length and strong ETag and identical body hash, and Content-Type remains application/javascript. If any variant differs in body hash, Content-Length, or introduces query-dependent content, classify as potentially dynamic and treat as non-testable under this methodology. Evidence to retain: request variant list, response codes, header sets, Content-Length/ETag values, body hash per variant, and decision rationale. ## Hypothesis Generation Framework Each hypothesis includes: known prerequisites, explicit assumptions, unknowns, and concrete future supporting or refuting checks. Illustrative payloads and checklists are provided as examples, not observed results. ### H1: Supply Chain Integrity Risk Hypothesis: The static vendor script could be tampered in transit or at the vendor host, leading to unexpected code execution in users' browsers. Prerequisites: - Asset is fetched from a third-party origin. - No Subresource Integrity attribute is present on the referencing <script> tag. - Response is served over HTTPS. Assumptions: - Browser will execute the script as referenced. - The referencing page does not apply additional integrity checks via Content Security Policy. Unknowns: - Whether integrity attribute is present. - Whether CORS headers allow integrity verification. - Whether the vendor host is trusted by policy. Future supporting checks: 1. Retrieve the referencing HTML and inspect <script src=...> for integrity attribute and crossorigin attribute. 2. Perform GET for the asset and record Content-Type, Content-Security-Policy, Access-Control-Allow-Origin. 3. Compute a local hash of the retrieved bytes and compare to a known-good hash from vendor documentation if available. 4. Check for Integrity-Policy or Integrity-Policy-Report-Only headers on the origin. Future refuting checks: 1. Integrity attribute present with strong hash algorithm sha384 or sha512 and crossorigin anonymous. 2. CSP with script-src 'strict-dynamic' and nonces limits execution. 3. Vendor provides signed release artifacts matching the served bytes. Illustrative checklist: - [ ] Script tag source URL captured - [ ] integrity attribute value captured - [ ] crossorigin attribute captured - [ ] Response headers captured - [ ] Hash computed ### H2: MIME Type and Content Handling Risk Hypothesis: The asset is served with an incorrect or permissive MIME type leading to browser misinterpretation. Prerequisites: - Asset is served with Content-Type application/javascript. Assumptions: - Browser uses MIME type to decide execution. Unknowns: - Whether the server also sends X-Content-Type-Options nosniff. - Whether the asset contains polyglot content. Future supporting checks: 1. Issue GET and record Content-Type, X-Content-Type-Options. 2. Inspect first bytes for shebang or non-JavaScript content. 3. Test with curl -I to confirm headers. Future refuting checks: 1. Content-Type is application/javascript and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff present. 2. Body parses as valid JavaScript without embedded HTML. Illustrative payload example for header check: ```bash curl -sI https://example.com/vendor.js ``` ### H3: Static Asset Versioning and Staleness Risk Hypothesis: The vendor script is outdated and contains known vulnerable patterns. Prerequisites: - Asset URL contains version identifier or is known to be vendor library. Assumptions: - Version can be inferred from URL or file content. Unknowns: - Actual library version. - Whether the version is supported. Future supporting checks: 1. Extract version string from URL or banner comment. 2. Compare version to vendor release notes for known issues. 3. Search file for deprecated APIs. Future refuting checks: 1. Version is current and supported. 2. No deprecated APIs present. ### H4: Information Disclosure via Static Script Hypothesis: The static script contains hardcoded secrets, internal URLs, or comments revealing internal architecture. Prerequisites: - Asset is readable without authentication. Assumptions: - Static analysis of bytes is sufficient. Unknowns: - Whether secrets are real or redacted examples. Future supporting checks: 1. Grep for patterns: API keys, tokens, internal hostnames. 2. Review comments for internal endpoints. Future refuting checks: 1. No high-entropy secrets found. 2. Comments are generic. ## Non-Testable Disposition Guidance A static asset can be considered non-testable for this methodology when: 1. Asset is not accessible via GET within scope, e.g., requires authentication. Evidence required: HTTP 401/403 response or scope exclusion. 2. Asset fails static-serving prerequisite verification. Evidence required: Prerequisite verification record showing variant requests with differing body hash, Content-Length, or ETag, or presence of query/path parameters that alter response. Decision rule documented above must be applied and result recorded. 3. MIME type is not application/javascript. Evidence required: Content-Type header value. 4. Asset is behind a bot protection or requires JavaScript execution to retrieve. Evidence required: Response indicates challenge page. 5. Legal or policy restriction prohibits fetching third-party vendor assets. Evidence required: Scope document excerpt. For a no_testable_hypotheses disposition, record: - Asset URL and discovery method - Reason for non-testability - Evidence collected: request method, response code, headers, prerequisite verification results including variant header sets and hash comparisons - Decision rationale referencing prerequisites above ## Operational Controls and Evidence Handling - Distinguish illustrative payloads and checklists from observed results. Do not record target-specific findings. - All checks are future validation steps. - Preserve uncertainty: mark unknown target conditions as future checks. - Use owned test environment for any active checks. - Retain only metadata about checks performed, not asset contents. ## Limitations This methodology addresses static asset review only. It does not cover dynamic script behavior, DOM interaction, or runtime vulnerabilities. Hypothesis generation does not prove vulnerability. Future validation requires target-specific execution and policy confirmation.
